sources.institution: U.S. House of Representatives: History, Art & Archives

evidence.representacao: Election to Congress and the 1972 presidential campaign provide direct evidence for electoral-democratic participation and expanded representation.
evidence.moral: Her campaign and legislative priorities emphasize racial and gender equality, relevant to the social-progressive side.
evidence.economia: House biography and policy record point to anti-poverty, education and social-program commitments; map public/private and planning/market axes after policy review.
evidence.imigracao: Do not infer immigration placement from civil-rights politics alone; seek issue-specific material before scoring.
evidence.estrutura: Chisholm worked through federal legislative institutions while representing a local Brooklyn constituency; her record supports national civil-rights and social-policy action without a distinct centralization doctrine.
evidence.poder: Her civil-rights, anti-discrimination and criminal-justice concerns support constitutional protections against unequal state power while retaining ordinary public institutions.
evidence.diplomacia: Her congressional record was internationalist and generally skeptical of militarized priorities, favoring diplomacy and domestic social investment.
evidence.intervencao: She opposed the Vietnam War and redirected attention toward social spending, supporting a relatively non-interventionist orientation.
evidence.controle: Her anti-poverty and social-program agenda supports meaningful regulation and public provision without command planning.
evidence.comercio: No reliable trade-policy doctrine is established from the reviewed sources.
evidence.religiao: Her public program was civic and egalitarian rather than religiously governed; no basis for theocracy is established.
evidence.tecnologia: No distinctive technology doctrine is established.
